messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arjun had never believed the city could turn against him until the Tuesday evening he took a shortcut through a narrow service alley behind a downtown loft conversion. A man stepped from the shadows, pressing the cold edge of a knife to his ribs and demanding his wallet. Arjun’s hands went numb, his breath hitched, and he fumbled for his keys while the robber snatched his phone and vanished into the damp dark. The assault lasted minutes, but its architecture lodged permanently in his mind. He remembers the scuff of the attacker’s boots and the glint of steel, yet the moments leading up to the confrontation remain a blur. When he tries deliberately to piece together the timeline, the details slip away, leaving him to sit with a crushing guilt on recall. He is certain he should have fought back or run faster, blaming his own hesitation for his vulnerability. That night, he began waking up from nightmares, sheets tangled around his legs, his heart hammering against his ribs as if the blade were still there. The attack rewired his daily existence, and the incomplete picture of what happened told him he was fundamentally defenseless, which hardened his negative appraisals into rigid rules: people can’t be trusted, and he can’t rely on others. This conviction isolated him, cementing his belief that no one would step in when the knife came out. His isolation then made him hyper-vigilant, ensuring that even routine contractor conversations sparked immediate threat detection. Unbidden recollections of the knife’s glint jolted him back to the alley’s narrow walls, turning every dimly lit corridor on his painting job sites into a spatial trigger. He began scanning for danger as he climbed ladders to prime high walls, his body constantly on alert, shoulders hiking up even when the space was empty. This mounting physical alarm frayed his patience; when his wife, Priya, asked him to leave his phone on the counter, he exploded into anger, convinced she was testing his readiness. He avoided crowded supply stores and spent his evenings alone in his truck, mistaking avoidance for safety. As the months passed, the loop tightened. Every time a delivery door slammed behind him or a figure stepped into his periphery, it acted as a trigger, flooding his system with physical threat. The sheer exhaustion of constant readiness sharpened his perception, making every flickering streetlight instantly potent and feeding the alarm. That physical threat response primed his nervous system for violence, which in turn pulled the fragmented memory of the alley forward again. The unbidden flash of a shadow against a primed wall pulled the memory of the event to mind suddenly, and because he could not deliberately recall what was missing, the guilt on recall reinforced his conviction that he was alone in a hostile world. When he clung to these negative appraisals, his scanning intensified and his irritability spilled onto coworkers, locking him deeper into the cycle. The more he tried to control the danger, the more his body braced for it, ensuring that each new trigger immediately revived the intrusion, which then confirmed his belief that he couldn’t rely on anyone. By the time Arjun finally scheduled an intake, he was exhausted, his marriage strained by his withdrawn demeanor, and his work suffering because he refused to enter basements or narrow hallways. He sat in the clinician’s office, hands clasped tightly, terrified that speaking about the alley would lock the fear in place forever. What he hoped for, more than anything, was a way to step out of the constant state of readiness and reclaim the trust that had been stripped from him.
